I've read REQ-405 and its transcript, and checked the evidence from your two latest runs. The short version: the guidance on story and quality exists, but none of it reaches the consultant at the moment it matters, and REQ-405's finish line for "Getting to know you" leaves the story out.

## REQ-405

The reframe was right. A finish line for each stage is a better fix than one more check that falls due, and "Bob can't ask for what he doesn't know exists" is the principle behind it.

**My main comment is that the finish line for "Getting to know you" is the wrong one.** As written, the consultant is done once she can say in two sentences what the business does, who it's for, what the site must do and what good means to the client. All four are facts. A Bob's Salon site and a Supercuts site could both meet them. What's missing is the one thing your question is about: **what's true of this business that isn't true of the one down the street.**

That used to be its own stage. DOC-33's Stage 2, "Positioning & differentiation", has the gate *"the client recognises themselves in it"*. Its instruction is plain: *"The AI's job here is interrogation, not generation… do not manufacture a differentiator."* When we collapsed DOC-33's stages into the seven on the progress bar, Stage 2 was dropped and nothing replaced it. Finding 13 had already shown it never ran in LF either.

I'd add a fifth line to the finish line: **you can name, in the client's own words, what's true of them that isn't true of their competitors, and they recognise it.** DOC-33's honest way out should stay too. If there genuinely isn't anything, say so, agree that the site's job is to be the most trustworthy and easiest to contact in the area, and record that as a decision. That's a finish line as well; skipping the question isn't.

One smaller thing: the `motion_offer` check still has a trigger that nothing ever fires. REQ-405 left it in place deliberately, but the data is now dead. It should either get a real trigger or be removed.

## Getting the story out

**What Bob's Salon shows.** The consultant asked one good question, *"Tell me about a typical week at the salon"*. Then you pasted 4,000 characters of background and it went straight to building. The best material, Dolores on Broadway and your mother doing reception, arrived only because you volunteered it, mixed in with your reaction to the competitor sites. When it did arrive, she recognised it at once (*"You've got a real story here"*) and wrote the site around it. So she can work with a story. She just won't go looking for one. A real Bob would have typed "we do cuts and colour, prices are on the board", and she would have moved on.

**So how do we square the circle?** I don't think it's a trade between time spent and quality. Six ideas, roughly in order of cost:

1. **Ask for stories, not adjectives.** "What makes you different?" gets "quality, friendly service", which is the professional-and-corporate answer you're worried about. Questions about a specific episode get stories:
   - *Why did you start?*
   - *Who came in last week and left happy?*
   - *What do you refuse to do that other salons do?*
   - *What do your customers tell their friends about you?*

   Ask them one at a time, which is already the rule. That's how a journalist interviews, and it costs nothing.
2. **Use the comps to make the case.** That stage is the natural place to have the conversation. *"All four of these say 'professional, friendly service'. So what's true of you that isn't true of them?"* It shows the client why we're asking, and it answers their pull towards looking corporate with evidence instead of an opinion. That also folds the old Stage 2 into the comps stage rather than adding a stage.
3. **Explain why she's asking, honestly.** *"I can't walk into your shop, so I need you to tell me what I'd notice if I did."* That helps with the not-talking-to-a-human problem: it gives the client a reason to tell her things.
4. **Let the draft do the asking.** People react far more easily than they come up with things, which was CHAT-21's point about plausible-but-wrong real English. A first draft carrying a guessed story line, clearly marked as a guess and never published unapproved (REQ-389's guard), gets corrected: *"no, I opened in 2009 after…"*. The draft can come early because it becomes the interview.
5. **Ask during the waits.** The ten-to-fifteen-minute builds are dead time. Put two or three story questions on the panel as optional free-text answers (REQ-390 added multi-line), and point to them in the status line before a build. That's the parallelism you described: the story gets gathered while the site gets built.
6. **Read what other people have said.** She has web search now. A real business's Google, Yelp or Facebook reviews are its customers telling its story in their own words, with no typing from the client. She can also suggest voice dictation, since talking is far easier than typing for a story. A microphone button on the composer would be a later product change.

**On her telling Bob what he knows and doesn't know: you're right.** It reads as condescending. The register rule should be to say what she needs and why, never what the client lacks.

## Does she judge her own work?

**No, and the reason is the same one again.** The thinking exists, and it's good. DOC-48 has the diagnostic:

> *"Strip out the copy. Swap the photographs for someone else's. Is the architecture still generic — could this be any business in any industry?"*

It also lists the tells that read as expensive and the ones that read as a template, and it has §12.3, *"A content vacuum, which no amount of design will fill"*, which is your story point exactly.

What happened in practice:
- **DOC-48 was never opened**, in Bob's Salon or in Charlie 3.
- **In Bob's Salon she didn't open any document at all.**
- **Her priming contains none of** *distinct*, *generic*, *unique*, *critique* or *assess*, and "story" appears once.

It's Finding 13 again: guidance that sits in a document she has to go and look up doesn't get used.

What I'd do:
- **A short rubric in the priming**, six lines distilled from DOC-48:
  - **The swap test:** take the copy and photos out; could this be any business in any industry?
  - **The headline test:** would it work for a different trade?
  - **One thing only this business could say,** visible on the home page.
  - **Real proof:** photos, names, reviews.
  - **The client's main action** in the first screen, at every width.
  - **Restraint:** a held palette and a type system, not defaults.
- **The host makes her use it.** A review check falls due when the first draft finishes and again before publishing, both triggers that already fire. It asks her to review against the rubric and tell the client the weakest point and what she'd do about it. That turns the "is this really premium?" question you keep having to ask into something the system asks. It's the interrogator role from the Bob discussion, done by the host at fixed points rather than by a second agent.
- **She acts on what she finds.** If the story test fails, she reopens "Getting to know you". REQ-390 already allows going back a stage, so circling back is a normal move rather than a failure.

A separate critic, such as a cheap second model reading the draft against the rubric, is a possible later step if self-review proves too lenient. I'd start with the self-review the host forces, and measure it first.

The consultant even told Bob *"none of your competitors show proof from real clients… your Wigs for Kids wall alone beats all of them on that"*, then never asked whether he had reviews of his own. Every real small business has some on Google or Yelp.
- **The best story lines.** "Growing it out, I'll plan it with you a year ahead", "What I did last week", and *"When they get up, they're not scared anymore. That's the job."* She never asked anything they would answer.
- **What did arrive** got there because you pasted it unprompted: the canon facts, the menu, and Dolores, mixed into your reaction to the comp sites.

To be fair to her, your README says material only counts once Bob says it in character, so she couldn't know about files nobody mentioned. But that's exactly the real situation. **She has no checklist of what a business usually already has** (reviews, photos of the work, the team, a logo, an old site, social pages, flyers, a price list), so she never asks for any of it. It's a cheap fix: one early question about what material the business has, plus searching the web for their reviews, which she can now do.

## The expert framing

Yes, with two adjustments.

- **State the bar, not just the title.** "You're a top web designer" on its own mostly makes a model more confident, not better. Pair it with the job: *"a site that could only be this business, which a template cannot do."*
- **"Professional" is the floor, not the aim.** Every template site already looks professional, and aiming there is the corporate trap you described. It's fine for her to tell a client their site will look professional, but she shouldn't make it the goal.

One risk: an "expert" persona will make the condescension you noticed worse. So the same paragraph should say that **experts ask more than they tell**.

## The story board: I think you're right

It's a better idea than my draft-as-interview, and it answers your concern about it.

- **Nothing on it can be made up.** A note is the client's own words, quoted and pinned, while a draft has invented copy. A novice looks at their own sentences and sees they were heard, instead of seeing AI text that's wrong about them. That's the property that makes it safe early.
- **It's the listening, made visible.** That addresses "I'm talking to an AI, why would I tell it my story?" Each answer appears as a note on the board, which is the reward for telling it. The board filling up is progress the client can see in the stage that currently shows them nothing.
- **It goes in the empty preview.** Before a draft exists the preview is a grey panel saying the site will appear there. That's the right space at exactly the right time. After the first draft, the board stays one click away. It's the record the copy is written from, not something you use once and lose.
- **It's separate from "What you've told us".** That section holds facts (phone, hours, prices). The board holds the story, with three kinds of note:
  - **quotes**, word for word, such as *"Long hair is long hair, it doesn't know if you're a boy"*;
  - **proof**, such as a review or the Wigs for Kids wall;
  - **people**: Bob, his mother, Marisol, Twee and Aoife.
- **The consultant groups them into themes**, such as "Long hair, kept long", "Priced by the hair, not the person" and "The neighbourhood". At the centre goes one card: her draft of what makes them different.
- **The client reacts to the notes**: a star for "that's us", a cross for "not that". A starred centre card is the finish line for "Getting to know you" that REQ-405 lacked: the client recognising themselves, which is DOC-33's Stage 2 gate, now visible.
- **It feeds the build.** Copy is written from starred notes, and the rubric's "one thing only this business could say" test is checked against the centre card.

**On making it fun:** Post-its are cheap and worth it. That means a yellow paper colour, a handwriting font, slight random tilts, and a small icon on each note for its kind (quote, proof, person). Arrows from each note to its theme and from each theme to the centre are a simple drawing job. What I'd keep out of the first version is a free canvas where notes can be dragged anywhere: that's a big UI build for little gain. Clusters around a centre give you the whiteboard feel without it. Hand-drawn pictograms per theme could come later from image generation, but icons are enough to begin with.

## How I'd split it

- **Prompt and seed changes, no code:**
  - the expert framing and its bar;
  - the new finish line for "Getting to know you";
  - asking for stories, not adjectives;
  - the "what have you already got?" question, plus searching for reviews;
  - the rubric, with the host-triggered review at first draft and before publishing;
  - the register rule.

  These could go into your next run straight away.
- **One REQ for the story board:** where it's stored in the plan, the consultant's operation for pinning and grouping notes, the board in the preview, and starring and crossing out.

- ❤️ **"That's us."** The heart of the business: the strongest candidates for headlines and the home page.
- 👍 **True, keep it.** Usable copy.
- 👎 **Not right, or not how I'd say it.** The note stays on the board, marked, and the consultant asks about it or offers a better wording.
- 🗑 **Delete: it doesn't belong.** It's removed from the board.

**Adding a note.** Clicking a theme lets the client type a note straight into it.

**Prompting the client.** After each batch of notes, the consultant says one line in the chat, e.g. *"I've put four of your sayings on the story board — heart the ones that are most you, and thumbs-down anything that's off."*

#### Claude
I think the trap is the word "statement". What you spent hours on in strategy sessions is a different object from what we need, and the difference is what makes ours cheap.

## What question it answers

**A strategy statement answers "what is this business?"** It's written for the owners and the staff. It has to cover everything the business does, for every audience, for years, and that's why it takes hours: every word has to carry the whole company.

**Ours answers a much smaller question: "why would the right customer pick you over the alternative they'd otherwise choose?"** It's read by a stranger in the first few seconds on the home page. It doesn't have to be complete or permanent. It only has to make the right visitor think "that's for me." For Bob it's not "Bob's Salon provides inclusive hair and beauty services to the South Boston community." It's *"Long hair, cut by people who'll keep it long."*

## What it's for

1. **The home page's opening line.** It's the hero headline or the line under it. That alone justifies having it.
2. **The yardstick for everything else.** Each section either supports it or is padding. This is the rubric's "one thing only this business could say", made concrete: the consultant checks the draft against a sentence the client chose, not against her own taste.
3. **The brief for every builder.** A single line tells a Haiku builder what the page is about better than a paragraph of instructions.
4. **The short copy elsewhere:** the share card's description, a Google Business profile, the line under the logo.

## How much effort it's worth

**One exchange, not a workshop.** The evidence for that is Bob's Salon itself. Once you'd pasted the background, the consultant produced *"Long hair, cut by people who'll keep it long"* in one turn, from your own sentences. When the material is there, it's cheap. It's hard only when the material isn't there, and then working on the wording won't fix it: the empty board is telling you there's no story yet. DOC-33's honest fallback then applies: say so, and make the site's job to be the most trustworthy and easiest to contact.

So the rules I'd set:
- **It's never written from nothing.** It only appears once the board has hearted notes, and it's built from them. Often it's nearly a client quote already: *"price by the hair, not the person"* is Bob's own phrase.
- **She offers two or three candidates and the client picks.** The client never drafts it, which is the same lesson as building looks rather than describing them. Picking is cheap, and choosing between real options is what novices are good at.
- **The client can edit their pick,** like any note.
- **It isn't locked.** It's the best line so far. It goes into the first draft, and if the client reads the hero and winces, it changes. The site is the test.
- **If nothing lands after one round, she skips it.** The headline gets settled in the draft instead, and nothing blocks.

## On the board

I'd make it a distinct card above the themes, not a central note. It's of a different kind from the notes: written by the consultant from them, not taken from the conversation. While she's offering candidates, the two or three appear there side by side, and the client hearts one. Once chosen, it's shown in the same type as the site's headline so it reads like the opening line it's going to be.

Two questions:
1. **What to call it.** "Statement" brings the strategy-session baggage. *"Why you"*, *"Your one line"* and *"The headline"* are all plain words. I lean to **"Why you"**, because it names the question rather than the format.
2. **Should a chosen "Why you" be part of the finish line for "Getting to know you"?** I'd say yes, with the skip counting: either the client picked a line, or she tried once and moved on. Either way the stage doesn't stall on it.

On your point 3: agreed. If the client can add notes they can edit them too, including the ones she pinned. An edited note becomes the client's wording, so the consultant no longer rewords it.

#### Claude
Here's how I'd lay the headline out, by state. It's one slot at the top of the board, always in the same place, so the client learns where it lives.

## The four states

**1. Empty.** Grey shadow text, *"The headline… why you?"*, the way a text box shows a hint. Clicking it lets the client type. We don't expect them to, but nothing stops them.

**2. Options offered.** This is the one that needs care. The slot shows the consultant's recommended option in full, in headline type, with a small strip under it:

> **Long hair, cut by people who'll keep it long.**
> ‹ 1 of 3 › · *my pick* · **Choose…**

- **‹ ›** steps through the options in place, so the client reads each at full size where it will sit. That's the same control as the looks band, so they already know it.
- ***my pick*** marks the one she recommends, so the client gets an opinion, not just a menu.
- **Choose…** opens a small selection panel with all the options stacked one above the other. Each has a "Use this" button, and **"Write my own"** is at the bottom. Seeing them side by side makes comparing easier than stepping through, and stepping is better for judging how each one reads alone. You need both, and they're one click apart.

While options are showing, the slot is visibly *undecided*: a dashed outline, and the strip present. Nobody should mistake an offer for a decision.

**3. Chosen.** The strip goes, and the line stands alone in headline type with a solid outline. Clicking it edits it in place. The unchosen options are kept in the plan as "offered, not chosen", so she doesn't offer them again.

**4. Edited by the client.** It looks the same as chosen, with a small *your words* mark. From then on it's the client's: she may suggest a change in the chat, but never overwrite it.

## Two rules that keep it honest

- **A new offer never replaces a choice.** If she has better options after the client has chosen, the chosen line stays, and the strip comes back as *"2 new options"*. The client opens them only if they want to.
- **Typing over an offer is a choice.** If the client starts editing while options are showing, their text becomes the headline and the options are dismissed.

She hears about a choice or an edit on her next turn, like a reaction. When she offers options, she says one line in the chat: *"I've put three headline options at the top of the story board — pick one, or write your own."*

## Two questions

1. **Does choosing a headline change the site straight away?** I'd say no. It's a decision on the board, and the consultant puts it into the hero on her next turn, where she can also fix the line underneath it. That keeps one rule: the client changes the board, and the consultant changes the site from it. The other option is immediate, which feels more magical but means a board edit silently rewrites the live draft.
2. **How should the headline look before the site has its fonts?** Before "Colours & fonts" there's no headline style yet. I'd use one neutral display face on the board, then switch to the site's own headline style once it exists. That way it previews how the line will actually look.

#### Claude
Agreed on both. The board is background material, and its look should come from its job, not from the site.

Here's a starting visual language where each visual choice carries meaning:

- **Colour means theme.** Each theme gets one note colour from a fixed, muted palette of six (yellow, blue, green, pink, orange, lilac), and the theme name is written on its cluster. Colour helps you spot a group at a glance, and the written name means it never relies on colour alone.
- **Emoji means what the note is about.** One per note, chosen by the consultant: 💇 for the work, 👪 for people, 💬 for something a customer said, 📍 for the place. It's how you'd scan a whiteboard for "where are the customer quotes?"
- **Size and weight mean the client's reaction:**
  - ❤️ notes are slightly larger and lifted, so the heart of the business stands out.
  - 👍 notes stay as they are.
  - 👎 notes go pale with the reaction badge showing, so they read as "to fix", not as gone.
  - Deleted notes leave the board.

  A glance at the board then shows what the client has said about it.
- **A handwritten feel, but legible.** The notes use a rounded informal face, not a scrawl, at a size you can read without zooming. A slight random tilt is the one purely decorative touch, and it's what keeps it from looking like a form.
- **The headline is written like marker on the board**: bigger, darker and plain, so it reads as the title of the whole thing, not as another note.
- **A calm background**: an off-white board with nothing on it but the notes, so the content is the only thing that draws the eye.
- **Very little motion.** A note fades in when the consultant pins it, and that's all. It's useful because it shows what just arrived, and it's switched off under reduced motion.

The rule I'd write into the ticket is the one you gave: a visual element earns its place by telling the client something, or by making the board easier to read. Nothing is decorative beyond the paper feel. The style is fixed, the same for every business, and never takes on the site's colours or fonts.

That covers the design end to end:
- Story as a third mode beside View and Edit, opening by default before the first draft.
- Quotes pulled from the conversation, lightly reworded, with the original on hover.
- Up to about six themes, each a colour.
- An emoji per note.
- Reactions: heart, thumbs up, thumbs down and delete, one at a time per note.
- The client can add and edit notes.
- The headline slot, with options, ‹ › stepping, a selection panel and "write my own".
- The board feeds the consultant, never the site directly.
- The board's finish line becomes part of "Getting to know you".

Shall I file it as the story-board REQ under EPIC-19, and make the prompt-only changes we discussed earlier?

#### Claude
I've filed **REQ-412**, *"bin/deploy: deploy the platform fonts automatically when the mirror has changed"*. It's at `draft` under EPIC-19, high priority, 3 points, and the epic links to it.

**Why this is now cheap.** Fonts were kept out of normal deploys on purpose (REQ-315), because checking 1.35 GB of fonts for changes could add an hour to every deploy. But the font list, `fonts/platform.json`, already stores a fingerprint (sha256) for every one of its 7,132 font files. So deciding whether the fonts changed means comparing one small file, not re-reading every font.

**What the ticket asks for:**
1. **Each environment remembers which fonts it last received.** Ideally that record sits in the font store itself, so it can't disagree with what's really there.
2. **Every `bin/deploy` checks that record first.**
   - If nothing changed, the output says `platform fonts: unchanged` and the deploy carries on.
   - If something changed, or there's no record yet, the existing font upload runs. It already sends only the files that differ.
3. **A half-prepared font set stops the deploy** before anything ships, and the error says which command fixes it.
4. **Fonts upload before the apps**, so a new version is never serving pages whose fonts haven't arrived yet.
5. **The flags:**
   - `--dry-run` shows what would happen with the fonts and changes nothing.
   - `--fonts` still deploys fonts only.
   - A new `--no-fonts` skips the check, and warns if the fonts were actually out of date.

**One thing stays manual:** re-encoding the fonts with `1c fonts mirror` isn't part of the deploy, because it needs the google-fonts checkout. After an encoder fix like BUG-227 you still run that yourself. From then on, a normal deploy ships the result to whichever environment you deploy to.

Your working tree has the re-encoded `fonts/platform.json` uncommitted, from this morning's font re-encode. Commit it before production, so the production deploy, and REQ-412's check once it's built, work from the corrected font list.

## What the run shows

**The story interview lasted 19 minutes and never came back.** The consultant asked five good questions between 17:01 and 17:20: how the salon started, a customer who left happy, Marisol, whether names can be used, and what the site is for. Then she moved to the comparison sites, and for the remaining 50-odd turns she didn't ask a single question about the business. "Wigs" appears nowhere in the transcript. It's in your letterhead, the services list, the story file and a testimonial, but nothing she asked would have led Bob to it.

**Her questions went wide, not deep.** Each answer got the same treatment: praise ("that's a great story"), pin it on the board, then a new topic. Only once, with Marisol, did she ask a follow-up about something Bob had just said. A good interviewer works the other way: she picks up a specific detail, says why it matters, and asks the next question about that detail. "You said a guy walks in with hair past his shoulders and they want to take it all off. Who's the customer you're proudest of keeping long?" is the kind of question that leads to a Wigs for Kids story.

**Every turn handed the decision back to you.** Almost every reply after the first draft ends with a question about what she just did: "does it feel like your salon?", "does the order feel right?", "are you happy with the layout now?". None ends with what she'd do next and why. A novice answers "looks good", and then there's nothing for either of them to do. That's the moment you're describing as waiting for Bob to decide. The ideas that moved the site forward mostly came from you:
- doing another layout pass with the new photos;
- "do you think we have the right fonts? (Bob wouldn't know to ask this)";
- the logo being too small, which you've raised on every site;
- "let's step back";
- leading with the group shot.

So she reacts well, but she isn't working through a list of the things a novice wouldn't think to raise.

## The busy screen

I agree it's manageable, but only if the consultant manages it. Right now each surface (Story, the looks band, the comparison sites, the questions) is something the client has to find. The rule I'd set: **a surface should show up because the consultant brought it there**, saying where to look and what to do. Two things would make that possible:

1. **The consultant can steer what's on screen.** Give her a tool to switch the preview to the story board, a comparison site, the looks or the draft, and to highlight a question on the panel. Then she says *"I've put the board in front of you; heart the two that sound most like you"*, and the client doesn't need to know the modes exist. This is the most direct answer to "where do I look?", and it's a code change.
2. **She visibly uses the answers.** Whether answering a question does anything is a matter of trust. If she says *"Thanks for the hours. They're in the footer now"*, the client learns that answering matters. She currently gets told about each answer, but seldom mentions it.

## The consultant leading

You're right that she can't rely on the client to steer. Three changes to her behaviour:

1. **She ends each turn by leading.** If there's a decision only the client can make, she asks it. Otherwise she proposes the next step and says why: *"Next I'd make the logo larger. It's getting lost, and owners always notice that once it's live. Shall I, or is something else bothering you first?"*. Asking "does it look right?" on its own doesn't count.
2. **She keeps a list of what a novice won't raise:**
   - logo and name size
   - fonts
   - the site on a phone
   - address and directions
   - real photos instead of placeholders
   - the story so far
   - the rubric checks

   She raises the next unchecked item herself. REQ-408's self-review is part of this, but this goes further.
3. **She listens actively** when gathering the story:
   - repeat back a specific detail;
   - say what it will do on the site;
   - ask about that detail before moving on.

   She should also check a short list of areas a small-business story covers:
   - how it started
   - the signature craft
   - the people
   - the customers
   - **what they do for the neighbourhood**, which is where Wigs for Kids lives
   - what they refuse to do
   - a moment they're proud of

   An area with no notes on the board means she reopens the conversation, including during the long builds.

## How I'd make it stick

Instructions alone haven't held up: the earlier evidence was guidance followed in 2 of 102 turns. So the new rules should be backed by facts the system shows her, not just advice:
- **Story coverage on her per-turn notice.** Something like *"Story board: nothing yet on the neighbourhood or a proud moment"* is a fact the system can work out from the board.
- **The novice checklist on the plan,** with each item marked done as it's handled, so "what next" is always something she can look up rather than remember.
- **A plain reminder that turns should end by leading.** This is the one piece that can't be enforced.

#### Claude
Agreed on steering, and having both is right: they're the same "show the client this" action, used two ways. Notes on your three ideas below.

## Steering: both ways

- **Switching the view itself** is the consultant's move when it has just made something to look at: *"The three looks are ready. I've put them in front of you."*
- **A link in the chat** is for when the client should choose the moment: *"[Open the story board](…) when you have a minute"*. In the transcript, links are better because they keep working after a reload. An automatic switch only happens once.
- **One guard on switching:** if the client is in Edit mode with unsaved changes, or is reading a comparison site, the consultant offers a link instead of switching. Changing the view under someone mid-edit is the quickest way to lose their trust.

## 1. Turns that end half-finished

Two different causes produce those frustrating endings, and they need different fixes.

- **Running out of budget.** REQ-409 covers this: higher limits, and a turn that runs out continues by itself instead of asking. When I checked that ticket on the 19th it was ready to build but not yet built.
- **Asking permission for the obvious next step.** "Here's what I'd like to do, is that OK?" is the consultant passing the decision back when there's nothing to decide. My earlier "end each turn by proposing the next step" was incomplete. The rule should be:
  - **Finish a stage you can stand behind**: something whole the client can react to, like a draft, a set of looks, or a fixed problem. Not half a pass.
  - **Then say what's next and do it**, unless there's a real choice. *"Next I'm making the logo bigger, which owners always want once it's live. Tell me if you'd rather I did something else first."* The client can redirect, but doesn't have to approve.
  - **Ask only when the answer can change what gets built**, such as which look, which order, or what's true about the business.

  That keeps the size of each stage reasonable without finishing the site in one go.

## 2. The worker and the talker

I think this is the best version of the two-agent idea so far. It keeps what the coordinator design was trying to get (the client isn't blocked, and the conversation keeps going during a build), and drops what went wrong with it: a second personality, a second voice and register, a cheaper model holding the conversation, and the naming problem. To the client it's one consultant that keeps listening while it builds. That also fits DOC-66.

How I see it working:

- **The fork.** When a turn starts building, the running turn becomes the worker. A message from the client then goes to a talker session started from the same history. Most of that history is already cached, so the talker's first reply is fairly cheap.
- **What the talker can do.** It can hold the discovery conversation, add questions to the panel, add notes to the story board, record decisions, and show the client a view or a link. It can't write to the site, start builders, or change anything the worker has locked. EPIC-24's locks already enforce that last part.
- **Information flows both ways while they run in parallel.**
  - **Talker to worker:** what the talker heard reaches the worker between its tool calls, through the per-request signals channel LF REQ-180 already built: *"While you've been building, the client said they'd rather lead with the group shot."* The worker decides whether to act on it now or after it finishes.
  - **Worker to talker:** the talker can see the worker's progress notes and milestones, so *"how's it going?"* gets a real answer, not a guess.
- **Interrupting.** The talker can stop the worker, but only when the client asks it to, as with the stop button. A client saying "I don't like this direction" should get *"Shall I stop the build and rethink?"*, not an automatic stop.
- **Merging.** When the worker finishes or is stopped, the two sets of messages are combined into one transcript in time order, and the next turn starts from it as a single agent again. The worker's live context can't be changed after the fact, but it doesn't have to be. It has already received the talker's points as signals, and the next turn starts from the combined transcript.

Three risks to design for:

1. **The talker promising things.** It could say *"Sure, I'll make it blue"* while the worker is building it green. The rule: the talker records and passes requests on (*"I've passed that on, and it'll be in the next pass"*). It never promises a change to the site during a build. Only the worker, or the merged agent afterwards, does that.
2. **Two voices that don't match.** If it's the same model with the same priming and the same history, it should sound the same. I'd keep the talker on the same model to start with. A cheaper talker is something to tune later, not part of the design.
3. **Cost.** Talker turns are extra spend. But each one replaces a client sitting idle for 15 minutes, and that's the cost your decision about turn budgets says matters.

Where it belongs: it's a framework capability, because it's about how a session is run, so it would be a lagrange-framework epic. It overlaps heavily with EPIC-7 (getting messages into a running turn) and with the two-speed room from EPIC-2, and could replace parts of both. The talker-to-worker signals and the stop control are already built. The new parts are the fork, the talker's restricted tools, and the merge.

## 3. Uploads as attachments

Agreed, the composer is the right place. Today a dropped file shows up in the chat as if it were a message, but the consultant doesn't see it until the client sends the next message, so it looks ignored. As attachments:

- **The file appears as a chip in the composer**: *IMAGE-12 · for the site*. Choosing whether it's for the site or for reference happens right there, which also covers what BUG-196 did on the panel.
- **It goes out with the next message**, so the consultant sees the file and the words together: *"here's the shopfront, can we use this at the top?"*.
- **Sending files with no text is allowed**, and gets a short reply: *"Got it, four portraits. Want them in the team section?"*.
- **Uploads answering a panel question** stay as they are. They're answers, and they reach the consultant through the notice it gets each turn.
- **The client's own edits in Edit mode** don't need a reply of their own either. The consultant already hears about them at the start of each turn.

## Once you say go

1. **Prompt changes, no ticket:**
   - finish a stage you can stand behind, then state the next step and start it, asking only when there's a real choice;
   - keep a checklist of what a novice won't think to raise;
   - listen actively and cover the main parts of the business's story.
2. **One 1stcontact REQ for steering:** the consultant switches the view, with the editing guard, plus view links in the chat.
3. **One 1stcontact REQ for attachments in the composer.**
4. **A lagrange-framework epic for the worker and the talker**, written as a design to discuss first, and cross-linked with EPIC-7.
5. **A finding on EPIC-19** covering the Bob's salon 2 evidence and these decisions.

Is REQ-409's automatic continuation the right home for the budget half of point 1, or do you want it handled differently?

#### Claude
I traced it. Your point 2 was already designed and built, and a bug stopped it from working.

## What should have happened

REQ-250 decided this exact case. Publish stays clickable, and when the site has no address the builder shows **a dialog** instead of the yellow failure banner. The dialog says what's missing and has a button that opens the web-address section in Settings. The reasoning in `publish-address.js`: someone who reaches this point "is by definition the one who does not know what a web address is", so a refusal has to come with the way out.

## Why you got the banner instead

The builder publishes in streaming mode, so it can show progress while pictures are resized. In that mode the server sends "OK" immediately and only checks the address after the stream has started. The refusal then comes back as the stream's last message, which carries the error text but drops the `NO_PUBLIC_ADDRESS` code (`router.ts` around line 8238). Without the code, the builder doesn't know it's the no-address case, so it falls back to the generic banner and shows the server's raw sentence, site id included. The comments in `api.js` assume the address is checked before the stream starts, but it isn't.

## Your three points

**1. The consultant didn't make it clear.** Agreed. Choosing a web address should be an explicit step in "Ready to publish", and asked before the consultant tells you to press Publish, not discovered afterwards. Two changes:
- **Prompt:** in Finishing touches, the consultant checks whether the site has a web address. If it doesn't, it explains in one line what a free `….1stc.site` address is versus your own domain, and gives you a link to the Settings web-address section, not a description of where to find it.
- **The link itself** is a natural extra target for REQ-413, which is still a draft: Settings, web-address section. I'd add it there rather than file a new ticket.
- **The consultant needs the fact.** Prompting alone won't make it remember. The notice it gets each turn should state "public address: none" once the site is near publishing, which is the same lesson as Finding 13.

**2. Disabled button or a popup.** I'd keep REQ-250's choice: a popup that says what to do, with the button straight to Settings. A greyed-out Publish gives a novice no reason and nothing to click. The dialog also stays correct when the rule changes, because it's driven by the server's answer. If you want a hint *before* the click, the safe version is a small "Needs a web address" next to Publish, based on the same check the server makes, not a second copy of the rule in the browser.

**3. Friendlier errors.** The banner shows whatever sentence the server produced, which is how a site id reached you. I'd set a rule: **an error the client can see never contains an id, a code or our internal terms.** Each refusal the client can act on has its own wording and an action. Anything unexpected gets a plain line, something like *"Something went wrong publishing your site. Try again in a minute, and tell us if it keeps happening."*, with the technical details behind a "Details" toggle for us. The publish banner is where to start, and it's worth checking the builder's other failure banners against the same rule.

## What I'd file

- **One bug:**
  - check the address *before* the publish stream starts, so it comes back as the proper refusal and the dialog appears, and send the code in the stream's last message too as a fallback;
  - give the publish banner the friendly wording, with details hidden;
  - add a test that publishing through the streaming path with no address opens the dialog.
- **Add the Settings web-address target to REQ-413.**
- **Prompt change, no ticket:** the web-address step before Publish.
- **Code to follow later:** the "no public address" fact in the consultant's per-turn notice, together with the novice-checklist facts from Finding 21, since they're the same kind of change.

**The rule is already in its instructions.** REQ-389's "Finish before you hand back" says *"Look at the result yourself, and fix what is visibly wrong in the same turn."* So this isn't missing guidance. **Four things push the other way:**

So the consultant leans towards not looking.
2. **It trusts the builder's report.** The builder says its checks passed, and BUG-225 showed builders answer checks from what they believe rather than from the page. A report saying everything passed reads as done.
3. **What it does see every turn is text.** The page digest lists sections and assets. A broken layout is fine in a digest; you only see it's broken in a picture.
4. **It may have looked at the wrong width.** If it took a desktop screenshot and you're viewing between the tablet and desktop layouts, a broken pricing grid at your width goes unseen. REQ-388 is meant to cover this, but it only helps if the consultant actually looks.

**The fix is for the host to do the looking, not the consultant.** After any builder session that writes a page, the host would:
- **Take the screenshot itself** at the width you're viewing, and attach it to the builder's result. The consultant then can't avoid seeing what was built.
- **Run a quick layout check** in the same browser render, and add any problems to the result as text. It would look for content running off the edge, boxes overlapping, clipped text, empty or collapsed sections, and a grid whose columns don't line up. That's cheap, objective, and works without anyone remembering to do it.
- **Treat a problem it finds as not done.** The consultant fixes it in the same turn before handing back, which uses REQ-409's continuation when that lands.

## Discovery while the worker builds

Yes, the talker can work on the story board. REQ-210 lets us choose which tools the talker is denied. Story-board pins, themes and headline options are plan writes, not site writes, so we'd allow them. Here's how I'd allocate the tools:

| talker **may** | talker **may not** (the worker's) |
|---|---|
| pin notes, group themes, offer headline options | write to the site, start builders |
| add panel questions, record your answers and facts | choose a look, make looks |
| add comps and record your likes and dislikes, web search (reviews) | publish, generate images |
| look at the site (read-only), report progress | move the progress stages |

**The flow that makes this efficient:**
1. **A short opening.** Ask just enough for a first draft: what the business is, who it's for, the main action, and one or two story details. Then start the build.
2. **Hand over with a question, not silence.** This is the key point. A talker only answers when you speak, so if the worker's last line is "about 15 minutes", you wait and nothing happens. The announcement before a build should end with the first story question: *"While I build, tell me how the salon started."* Your answer opens the talker, and the interview runs while the build does.
3. **The talker works through the story areas still missing,** one question at a time. It follows each answer up on a specific detail, pins what you say, and points you at panel questions when the story is covered. Its reminder each exchange lists which areas are still empty, so it knows what to ask next.
4. **What you said reaches the worker at its next tool call**, with the instruction not to reply. The rule: **new story goes into the next pass, not the build already running,** unless it contradicts something being built ("the shop's on Broadway, not Main Street"). The talker says so: *"That's going into the copy on the next pass."* That stops a mid-build U-turn and keeps the talker from promising changes.
5. **The worker's final result picks it up:** *"While I built, you told me about Dolores and the Wigs for Kids wall. The next pass puts both on the home page."*

## How to split the work

Discovery during builds changes what goes in each build. The guidance I'd give:
- **Build the structure and the look first, and write the story-heavy copy last.** The first draft uses only what's already known, with the copy clearly marked as a first version. Section headings and the layout don't depend on the interview, so they can go early. The headline, the about section and the proof wait for what the talker gathers.
- **Each pass ends with something whole you can react to**, and the next pass is shaped by both your reaction and what the talker gathered meanwhile.
- **Split each pass into independent sections** so builders run together (REQ-410/411). That shortens the wait, but the wait is also when the interview happens. That's fine: the talker's question list is the limit, not the build time.

## Decisions for you before I write the adoption ticket

1. **Should the talker be allowed to add notes to the story board while a builder is writing that same text?** I'd say yes. The board is background material and never touches the site directly.
2. **Should the talker be allowed to move the progress stages?** I'd say no. Stages follow the work, which is the worker's.
3. **Should the first build start sooner,** after the short opening, so the full story interview happens as a talker conversation? That's the biggest change to the method, and I think it's the right one.

#### Claude
These are three separate problems, and all are fixable. One more turned up while I was checking the pacing rules.

## 1. Too many photos hide the text box

The chips above the text box wrap onto as many rows as they need, with no height limit (`.builder-attach` in `builder.css:1263`: `flex-wrap: wrap`, no `max-height`). Add enough photos and the chips take over the composer and push the text box out of reach. **Fix:** the chips area gets a maximum height of about two rows and scrolls inside itself, or collapses to "+8 more". The text box and the Send button always stay visible and clickable, however many files are attached.

## 2. The consultant's turn was too much

It already has a rule that says *"keep to one topic and at most one question per message."* That turn broke it in three ways:
- **It listed every panel question in the chat.** The questions are already on the panel. Spelling them out puts five questions into one chat message, and that's what pulled you away. A line we added in REQ-401 ("announce every question you add") probably encouraged this.
- **It also said what's coming next** (comps, then the first draft).
- **The question that mattered most came last,** after everything else had already sent you off doing something.

**Fix, in the priming:**
- Questions added to the panel get **one line in total**: *"I've put a few quick questions on the panel above, whenever suits you."* Never one line per question, and never the questions themselves.
- **A message ends on its one real question, and that question is the main thing in it.** When the most important question is a story question, little else should be in the message with it.
- **"What happens next" goes in a separate message, or not at all,** when the message also asks something.
- The rule is to pace the conversation: one thing at a time, and the client's attention goes to the thing that matters most.

## 3. The worker's result arrived while you were replying to the talker

REQ-210 already holds the worker's result until the talker has finished its reply, but it doesn't know you were partway through typing. The real problem is the **page and a half.** The worker's result is written as a full report when it should be a hand-back. **Fix:**
- **The worker's result is short:** what's ready, where to look, and at most one question. About three lines. The details stay in its own record, and the consultant brings them up when relevant.

## 1. The name and logo too small

You've raised this on every site, and it's in the consultant's novice checklist ("the logo and the business name large enough to read"). It keeps happening for the reason we've now seen several times: builders default to modest sizes, and a checklist line in the priming is a reminder, not a check. The fix is the same pattern as REQ-415: **make it something the host measures.** The layout check already renders every page a builder writes, so it can also report:
- a header logo shorter than about **48px on desktop or 36px on a phone**;
- a business name in the header that **isn't clearly the largest text in it**, e.g. smaller than about 1.25× the navigation links.

Either finding means the build isn't done, the same as overflow. Builders also get a default to start from, instead of choosing a size themselves.

## 2. Heading and text spacing: you're right, and the cause is structural

What you're describing is the **proximity principle**, the most basic rule of typographic rhythm. Things that belong together sit closer together. A heading belongs to the text *below* it, so the space above a heading should be clearly larger than the space below it, typically **2–3 times** larger. When heading, paragraph and next heading are evenly spaced, the heading looks as if it floats between two blocks, and the page reads as a list of loose parts. That's the "something's off" feeling, and professional designers fix it before almost anything else.

**Why our sites keep doing it:** in our page format (L1), a container spaces its children with **one value, `gapPx`**, the same gap between every pair (`render.ts:5041`). A builder putting heading, paragraph, heading, paragraph in one stack can only space them evenly. It isn't a lapse of taste the builder could avoid. The simplest structure produces exactly what you're seeing.

Three ways to fix it, from cheapest to most thorough:
1. **Builder guidance:** each heading and its text go in their own small group with a tight gap, and the groups sit in an outer stack with a larger gap. That's possible today, but it depends on builders remembering, which we know is unreliable.
2. **A host layout check:** flag any heading whose space to the text below it isn't clearly smaller than its space to whatever is above it. That makes it a "not done" finding, like the others, so it can't slip through.
3. **Spacing that belongs to text styles:** a heading style carries its own space above and below, e.g. 2.5× above and 0.5× below the base unit. Every heading then gets the right rhythm automatically, and it holds across the whole site. This is the professional answer, in the same spirit as REQ-418's table: a structure in which the mistake can't be made. It's an L1 change.

**My recommendation:** do 1 and 2 now in one ticket together with the logo check, since they're the same kind of thing: craft defaults builders get wrong, which the host now measures. File 3 as an L1 request alongside REQ-418, because it removes the problem for good and saves the build-flag-repair cycle of tokens.

#### Claude
Agreed, this belongs in the language. And L1 already has most of what it needs: text runs know they're headings and at what level (REQ-269, `heading.level`), and sites have named text styles (REQ-350). **What's missing is any notion of vertical rhythm.** Spacing exists only as the container's single `gapPx`, so the language can't tell a heading attached to its paragraph from one floating between two blocks.

## The design I'd propose

**1. A rhythm unit for the site.** One base spacing unit, typically about the body text's line height, set alongside the type system and allowed to differ by width, so phone rhythm is tighter than desktop.

**2. Text styles carry their own space.** Each named style gains `spaceAbove` and `spaceBelow`, measured in rhythm units, typed and bounded like every other axis. Defaults come from heading level:

| | above | below |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | 3 | 0.75 |
| H2 | 2.5 | 0.5 |
| H3 | 2 | 0.5 |
| Body paragraph | 0 | 1 |

That puts the pairing in the language: a heading pulls the next text towards it and pushes the previous block away. **Every heading on every page gets it, without anyone remembering.**

**3. Stacks space by rhythm.** A stack's spacing mode becomes `rhythm` (or keeps today's uniform `gap` for card grids, image rows and buttons). In rhythm mode, the space between two neighbours is the **larger of** the first one's space below and the second one's space above, which is how typesetting has always worked. So heading → paragraph is tight, and paragraph → next heading is generous, because the heading's space above wins. The first child's space above is dropped at the top of a container, so section padding still controls the edge. Text-led stacks use rhythm by default.

**4. The AI can adjust it, locally.** A node can override its space above or below, in units, for a specific need such as a hero headline sitting tight under an eyebrow line. Changing the style changes every use; an override changes one.

**5. Keep-with-next.** Headings are kept with the content they introduce when a layout reflows (columns stacking on a phone, a card breaking). The renderer also emits the semantic grouping, so a screen reader hears the heading and its text as one unit.

## What it touches beyond the schema

- **Validator and renderer:** spacing becomes collapsed margins between neighbours, not CSS `gap`. Everything is still structured, with no raw CSS.
- **Capture and fold:** when we reproduce a reference site, the fold has to *read* its rhythm, meaning the spacing above and below headings and paragraphs, and put it into the styles. Otherwise reproductions lose it. That's real work, and it matters for the round-trip guarantee.
- **Builders and the consultant:** taught to use rhythm stacks for text and to set spacing on styles, not per node.
- **Existing pages** keep `gapPx` and render exactly as now. They switch to rhythm when next restyled.

## Three decisions for you

1. **Implicit or explicit pairing?** I've proposed implicit: the pairing comes from the spacing on styles, plus keep-with-next. The alternative is an explicit "titled block" node that builders must create. Explicit is clearer to read, but it's one more structure builders can forget to use. The implicit version applies to every heading automatically, which I think is what you're after.
2. **Rule or default?** Should the language *forbid* a heading whose space below is greater than or equal to its space above, or make it the default and have REQ-415's layout check flag a violation? I lean towards default plus flag, because there are real designs (eyebrow labels, display headings) that break the rule deliberately.
3. **Where it goes.** It's L1, in `packages/site-schema` and the renderer here, so it's ours, not the framework's. I'd file one REQ under EPIC-19 (or whichever epic you treat as L1's home), next to REQ-418. The logo-size and heading-spacing layout checks would go in a separate small bug, since they help existing pages straight away.

#### Claude
I read it. Here's what happened, and how I'd use the parallelism.

## What happened

Your 00:38:37 message had two parts: **a request** (more movement, like the top photo) and **a question** ("what's next?"). The consultant's turn treated the whole message as a build request. Its first action was a builder call, and all you saw was the status note: *"Adding a gentle opening movement to the top photo and headline, about 5 minutes."* So your question had no answer. Sixteen seconds later you asked "What's next?" again, which opened a talker. The talker answered well: the plan in three steps, plus a good story question about Aoife's room. Then the worker finished and answered "Next: colours and fonts" a second time, repeating what the talker had just told you.

There are two defects:
1. **The worker went straight to work** without answering the conversational part of the message.
2. **The worker's hand-back repeated** something the talker had already answered. It's told about the talker's exchanges, but nothing tells it not to repeat them.

## Can we tell when the AI starts working? Yes, exactly

The host sees the moment a turn issues its **first tool the talker isn't allowed**, such as `Delegate` or a site write. That's the point where the turn has committed to building. If it does that **before writing anything to you**, it has gone into work mode without replying.

## Replaying your message to a talker: yes, that's the opportunity

When the worker starts building without replying, the host **immediately opens a talker on the same message**, with no second message needed from you. The talker is told that the worker has taken the building part (it's given the status note), and that its job is to:
- **answer anything else you asked**, in this case "what's next?";
- otherwise **acknowledge briefly and ask a story question**, which is exactly the hand-over REQ-416 wanted;
- **say nothing** if the message was purely a build request and there's nothing useful to add (that option has to exist, or it will always chatter).

This gets you three things at once:
- **No unanswered questions.** Mixed messages are common, and this splits them automatically: the worker builds, the talker replies within seconds.
- **The build-time conversation always starts.** Today, a talker only appears if you speak again. With this, every build opens with a talker turn, so the story interview starts by itself instead of relying on the worker remembering to end its announcement with a question.
- **It's cheap.** The talker shares the worker's cached prompt (REQ-210), so a quick reply costs little. Its value is exactly what you said earlier: it makes your waiting time useful.

## What it needs

1. **A framework addition** (lagrange-framework): a host can open a talker round on a **cue the client never sees**, answering the message that started the worker. Today a talker only opens on a new client message from the inbox (`talkerDesk` → `startTurn`).
2. **On our side:**
   - detect the moment the turn starts building before it has said anything to you, and open the cued talker;
   - give the talker the instruction above, including "say nothing if there's nothing to add";
   - add a rule to the worker's hand-back: **don't repeat what the talker has already told the client.** It already receives those exchanges.
3. **A cheap priming rule for now:** if a message both asks something and asks for work, answer the question in a line or two first, then start the work. It won't be reliable on its own (Finding 13), but it helps until the structural fix lands.

That's one lagrange-framework REQ for the hidden cue, and one 1stcontact ticket for the detection, the talker instruction, and the no-repeat rule. Shall I file them, and put the priming line in now?

#### Claude
Agreed on both. Here's how I'd shape it.

## The comp tile

Make each comp a proper card in the board, not a row:
- **The hero thumbnail**, larger, with the site name and "Open the real site ↗".
- **The consultant's note**: why this site was chosen, in a line or two (*"The odd one out: here to show how far 'premium' can go"*).
- **Your notes**: a real multi-line box that grows as you write, with a gentle prompt in it: *"What do you like? What would you never do?"*
- **A footer** with the box's state and the send button.

On a wide panel, two cards per row; otherwise one.

## "Done" really means "send", and the box needs states

You're right: today's Done saves silently and leaves you guessing whether anything happened. I'd give the box three visible states:

| state | what you see |
|---|---|
| **Empty** | the prompt text, and the button dimmed |
| **Unsent changes** | a small dot plus *"Not sent yet"*, and the button live: **Send to the consultant ➤** |
| **Sent** | the card's edge turns your accent colour, *"Sent ✓ 2:14pm"*, and the button dimmed. Edit again and it goes back to *"Not sent yet"* |

Your typing is still kept as a **draft** (on blur, and while you type), so nothing is ever lost. But a draft is visibly different from something sent, and only Send reaches the consultant. That separates "saved" from "said".

For consistency, the same states would apply to the panel's other typed answers, where the button reads **Save** because they don't start a conversation: *"Not saved yet"* → *"Saved ✓"*.

## Sending a comp note starts a short exchange

When you press Send:
1. The card changes to *Sent*.
2. Your note appears **in the chat as your own message**, labelled with the site: *"On JDS Custom Ironworks: love the photos of real jobs, can't stand the phone number in five places."* The conversation then has a record of it, and the consultant reads it in context.
3. **The consultant replies briefly**, two or three sentences at most: what it takes from your note for your site (*"Real job photos, yes. We'll use yours from the Saturday classes and the shipyard. One phone number, placed well."*), and **a follow-up question only if your answer opened something worth asking**. No summary of the comp and no list.
4. When you've sent notes on every comp, or pressed "I've finished commenting", the consultant **sums up** the conventions it will follow and records them as the visual-concept decision. That's the step the first draft is built from.

This replaces BUG-236's "I've finished commenting" ending with a natural one, and it fits the one-thread rule: your note *is* the thread, so the reply belongs right there. If a build is running, the talker answers, in the same voice.

One deliberate change: until now, panel answers never started a turn (DOC-65). Comp notes would be the exception, because they're opinions to react to, not facts to file. Phone, hours and the other fact questions keep the current behaviour.

## Three decisions

1. **Can a note be edited after it's sent?** I'd say yes. Editing makes it *Not sent yet* again, and re-sending posts the change as a new message.
2. **Should the consultant reply to every comp note, or only when there's something worth saying?** I'd say always, but very short. Silence after you've written something feels like being ignored, and it's an Opus turn per comp, which is fine for four or five comps.
3. **Should this go with last turn's items** (one thread at a time, comps as one line and a link, the "why chosen" commentary, new-question badges) **in one ticket?** I'd say yes, since it's all one experience. The consultant reply to comp notes and the panel's Save states would be listed as their own items.

Good, the reload confirmed it. I've added that to BUG-247: the fault is in the live chat's state for a turn that started by answering you, not in the server.

On the preview refreshes, the code explains all three:

**What happens now:** every time the site's change count goes up, the builder calls `panel.reloadDocument()` (`app.js:879`), which does a plain `location.reload()` of whichever page is showing. It doesn't check *which* page changed, and it doesn't remember where you'd scrolled to. And because a reload is a fresh page load, every entrance animation plays again.

**How I'd fix it:**
1. **Keep your scroll position.** Load the new version in a hidden frame, scroll it to where you were, then swap it in. The panel already has this machinery: it preloads looks in hidden frames and cross-fades between them (`SWAP_MS`). Refreshes would reuse it instead of reloading in place. This also removes the flash.
2. **Only refresh when *your* page changed.** The site-changed signal should say which pages changed. The page you're viewing refreshes only if it changed, or if something shared did (site styles, fonts, the header or footer, the palette). A builder working on the prices page leaves your home page alone.
3. **No entrance animations on a refresh.** A page loaded *because something changed* is rendered with entrance animations switched off. They still play when you open a page yourself, and there's an easy way to replay them, so movement can still be judged.
4. **Fewer refreshes during a burst of changes.** While a build is making many changes, refresh at most every few seconds, plus once when it finishes. You still watch the page grow, without constant redraws.

It's mostly browser-side, plus one change to the site-changed signal so it names the pages. Shall I file it as one bug under EPIC-19?

#### Claude
I looked, and I can't give you the cause. That's itself one of the problems.

**What the records show for `turn_cc6be6d1…`:**
- Your message reached the server at 18:29:05, and the reply stream opened normally (`POST /api/ai/prompt` → 200).
- **Nothing after that.** There's no error, warning or restart in the dev log. The turn's row in `turn_log` has **no end time and no outcome**, so as far as the server knows, the turn is still running.
- About two minutes later your browser reconnected (`/api/ai/session`), and then came your retries.

So the reply didn't fail with an error. **It stopped producing anything and was never closed.** The most likely cause is a model API call that stalled (the connection open, no bytes) with nothing timing it out. An isolate dying silently is possible, but there's no restart in the log. The browser's turn-health check noticed the silence and showed you that note. Nothing on the server ever recorded what went wrong.

## What robust looks like

1. **Retry at the request level, invisibly.** Every model call gets a **stall timeout** (no bytes for, say, 60 seconds) and **automatic retries with backoff** on transient failures: overloaded or 5xx responses, a dropped connection, a stall. Within a turn, the earlier tool results are already in the history, so retrying the last request repeats no work and you never notice. This belongs in lagrange-framework's `ClaudeAPIBackend`.
2. **If a turn still dies, pick the flow back up automatically.** The host resumes the turn instead of asking you to "ask again". It can use REQ-409's continuation, or the framework's resume-from-the-session-log work (LF REQ-175), so the client sees the reply carry on.
3. **No ugly messages for clients.** In production the client sees something like *"One moment, picking that back up…"*, while it retries. No turn ids and no "it was our failure, it has been recorded". In dev you keep the full detailed note, behind a dev setting.
4. **No turn left open.** A watchdog closes any turn with no activity for too long, recording an outcome such as `stalled` and its cause, so `turn_log` never has holes like this one.
5. **Every failure logs its cause:** the status code, how long it stalled, and which request. The next time this happens we'll know why.

I'd file this as **two tickets**:
- **lagrange-framework:** stall timeout plus transient retries in the API backend (item 1).
- **1stcontact:** automatic resume, client-facing wording with dev detail kept behind a dev setting, the turn watchdog, and failure logging (items 2–5).

Shall I file them?

#### Claude
Agreed, it would be catastrophic, and a restart fixing it makes it worse. A restart only clears memory inside one worker process. In production, leases and locks held in a Durable Object outlive that process, so a stuck session could stay stuck with nothing to restart. I've filed it as **BUG-249** (**critical**, 8 points, under EPIC-19).

**What happened, as far as the records show:** the turn started, then something inside our server waited on an operation that never finished. Candidates are a Durable Object call, a file lock, the background write to the session log, or the talker desk. Meanwhile its heartbeats kept saying "I'm alive", so the turn held its lease and every later message stayed blocked. No error was logged and the turn was never closed. The heartbeat proves the process is running, not that the turn is making progress, and that's the core flaw.

**What the ticket requires:**
1. **No turn can hang forever.** Each turn has a progress deadline: no new text, tool activity or progress for a configured time means the host aborts it. It records the outcome `stalled` with what it was waiting on, and releases everything it holds: the lease, file locks, draft leases, and the talker desk. Heartbeats don't count as progress. If that part lives in the framework, a lagrange-framework ticket gets filed for it.
2. **Leases and locks expire by themselves** once their holder stops making progress.
3. **The conversation picks back up automatically,** and your next message is never blocked by the dead turn.
4. **No unpleasant messages for clients.** Production shows *"One moment, picking that back up…"*; the detailed note with the turn id stays in dev.
5. **Every turn closes in `turn_log`** with an outcome and a cause, and a watchdog closes any left open.
6. **The cause is logged:** the last event and what was being waited on, so the next incident tells us why.
7. **Resilience to model API failures** (timeouts and retries), filed in the framework if it isn't already there.
8. **For production:** an alert when a turn stalls, and an admin "unstick this session" action as a last resort.

Very possibly, yes. In this run the logo is a hand-written SVG (`ariels-sign.svg` on the site), and drawing tools like that are on the builders' side, which run Haiku 4.5. I haven't confirmed which session wrote that particular file, but it fits a builder.

**Why a hand-drawn logo is hard for Haiku:** writing SVG paths by hand means planning shapes in coordinates, with no eyes on the result. It needs spatial reasoning (curves, proportions, optical balance) and design judgement at the same time. Larger models are much better at both. On xgd, the logo was probably drawn when the consultant (Opus) did the work itself, before most building was handed to builders. That would explain "moderately successful" there and worse here.

**Options, roughly from most to least promising:**
1. **Start with a wordmark.** Most small-business logos are a well-set name: a chosen typeface, weight, spacing and maybe one simple mark or rule. That's typography, which L1 already does well, and it's within reach for any model. It also stays crisp and editable. Make this the consultant's default.
2. **Give craft work to a stronger model.** A logo is small in tokens and large in impact, which is exactly the trade where paying for Opus or Sonnet is right. Either the consultant draws it itself, or `Delegate` gets a tier, e.g. `craft`, that runs on a stronger builder model for briefs like logos, illustrations and a hero composition. That's in keeping with your cost model: spend tokens where judgement matters.
3. **Illustrated marks come from image generation, not hand-written SVG.** `CreateImage` and `EditImage` already exist. The consultant writes the prompt, looks at the result, which counts as a look under REQ-415, and iterates with you. A raster logo is fine on the web at the right size. Converting it to vector can come later if it's ever needed.
4. **Always look at it.** The post-build screenshot (REQ-415) catches a bad mark, but only once it's on the page. For a logo, the consultant should check it on its own and at the header's actual size before anything else is built around it.

**My recommendation:** do 1 and 3 by default and 2 for anything hand-drawn, and never leave a logo to a Haiku builder working alone. That's one ticket: a model tier on `Delegate` (with the strong model set in configuration), plus the consultant's logo method in the priming. Shall I file it?

2. **It picked the story, not the sale.** *"If you wouldn't stand under it, don't weld it"* is the most vivid line on the board, and that's why it was chosen. But it answers "what's memorable about you?", not "why would a contractor choose you?". It's **evidence** (it belongs in "Where it started", or behind a claim about safety and code), not a **pitch**. Nothing in the consultant's method makes it look through the *buyer's* eyes: what does a contractor weigh when choosing a welder? Licensing, inspections, reliability, turnaround, capacity, and quality they can show their own client.
3. **There was no synthesis step.** The story board collects material. Nothing turns it into a position. So the consultant went from a pile of notes straight to a headline, and when that missed, back to asking you.

## Your approach 2 is the missing step: synthesise, then ask

Before any headline, the consultant should show its understanding as a short **positioning summary** you can react to:
> **What I'm hearing:** structural work done to code (permits, inspections, licensed), art and custom work nobody else will take on, and a shop with a family trade behind it.

## The spectrum: propose first, everywhere

For messaging, look and feel, and site functions, the same rule covers everyone from "I don't know where to start" to "just do what I tell you":

#### Claude
Yes, that's the right shape: an internal critic. It's a different kind of thing from the worker and the talker, though, and the details decide whether it helps.

## What the critic is

**A tool, not a participant.** The worker builds and the talker converses, and both face the client. The critic is an **internal audit**: a separate model call that assesses the work and hands its findings to the consultant. It never speaks in the chat. The consultant decides what to do with the findings and what to tell you, so there's still one voice.

**Its value is the clean, independent view.** The consultant goes wrong because its context is full of machinery and its own momentum. The critic gets:
- **only the brief and the result:** the positioning card, your hearted notes and decisions, the comps conventions, and screenshots of the pages at desktop and phone width;
- **none of the consultant's reasoning.** If it sees *why* something was done, it tends to agree with it. A critic that only sees the result judges it the way your customer will.

**Focused by lens**, each with its own short rubric (much of it already written in DOC-48):

| lens | asks |
|---|---|
| **Strategy** | Does the site serve the business's goal? Is the positioning clear? What's missing from the customer's path from landing to calling? |
| **Messaging** | Does the headline answer what the buyer is deciding on? Is every claim backed by proof? Could this text belong to a competitor? |
| **Style** | Hierarchy (is the name larger than the headings?), rhythm, contrast, brand presence, consistency between pages, the busyness the trade expects |
| **Function** | Contact routes, phone display, forms, navigation between pages, and checking that "it's in the menu" is actually true |

**Its output is short and ranked:** the top one to three findings, each with its severity, the evidence, and a suggested fix. It's allowed to say "good enough". Without that, it nitpicks forever.

## When it runs

- **At stage gates, triggered by the host, so it doesn't rely on anyone remembering:** strategy and messaging at the end of discovery, before the first build; all lenses after the first draft and again before publishing.
- **When the consultant asks:** for example, *"is this headline any good?"* before offering it to you.
- **While the worker builds:** it runs alongside, so it adds no waiting time.

## Rules that make it work

- **It runs on a strong model.** Judgement is the whole point, and a Haiku critic would be worse than none. That fits your cost model: one call per lens per gate, with shared inputs cached, is token spend that buys quality.
- **The consultant must respond to every top finding,** either by acting on it or by recording why not. Otherwise critiques get ignored, as rules have been.
- **Only the single weakest point reaches you.** It powers the existing weakest-point check from REQ-408 (*"Honestly, the weakest part of the site right now is… Shall I…?"*), so you're not buried in critique.
- **No loops.** A fixed number of critique rounds per gate, so it can't polish forever.
- **It's measurable.** Critic findings logged across runs become our quality metric: whether headline problems or hierarchy problems are getting rarer from one business to the next.

## Next step

It changes how the consultant thinks, so I'd **write the design note first**: a short DOC covering the critic's inputs, the lenses with their rubrics, the gates, the rules, and how it fits with the worker and talker. Then the tickets: probably one in lagrange-framework, if a critic call with a clean context is a general mechanism, plus one here for the lenses, gates and wiring. Shall I write the note?

## What would address conversation strategy

The same lesson as before applies: the consultant handles things well when they're a **fact in front of it**, and badly when it has to **remember to do them**. Conversation strategy is currently all memory. Two pieces would change that.

**1. The host works out the "next move" and states it every turn.** The plan already holds the material: the stages, open questions, notes and reactions, the positioning card (REQ-425), and your readiness per area. Simple, predictable rules can turn that into a line in the consultant's per-turn notes, for example:
> *Getting to know you: 14 notes, 0 reactions, no positioning card. Next move: a reaction task (REQ-424), then the positioning card. Don't ask for new material until then.*

or
> *Messaging readiness: has ideas. Propose a headline from the card; don't brainstorm.*

That turns "stop gathering, have them react, synthesise, then ask" from advice into state. It's cheap, the same every time, and testable.

**2. A strategist pass at stage boundaries.** Once per stage, a strong-model call with a clean context (the plan, the board, your readiness, how the conversation has gone so far) produces a short **conversation plan for the stage**: which decisions remain, in what order, how to approach each for *this* client, and where a focus task fits. That's essentially the **executive function** we designed Bob for, as a planner instead of a second voice. We dropped Bob because two voices in the chat didn't work; the job itself still needed doing.

**So there are two separate things:**
- **a conversation director** (host-computed next move, plus a strategist pass at stage gates) for how the dialogue is run;
- **the critic** (one review at the end of each big run) for whether the work is any good.
